food.text: The two main grains in Byzantine Anatolia were wheat and barley. Barley had a lower nutritional value than wheat and sold for a lower price, so Byzantine cooks valued it less.

Bread played a major part in the Byzantine diet, and the finest loaves were made from finely sieved wheat flour with no other grains mixed in. Cheaper breads combined wheat with rye, millet, egg yolks, or chickpeas.

Historians disagree about the average Byzantine diet in Anatolia. Some scholars argued ordinary people ate mainly bread, vegetables, and wine with little meat or fish, while Joanita Vroom argued that grains, dairy, fish, meat, olive oil, and honey were all part of a typical diet.
In Bagratid Armenia, the city of Ani grew into a major trading hub that exported salt, wine, honey, cattle, and horses. Its main trading partners included the Byzantine Empire and the Arab Caliphate.
Byzantine citizens slaughtered pigs at the beginning of winter to provide their families with food for the whole year. The pork was preserved as sausages, salt pork, and lard.

Lamb was a luxury in the Byzantine world, affordable mainly to the upper middle class and the wealthy. Beef was rarely eaten because cattle were needed to plow the fields rather than be slaughtered for meat.

Ani became the capital of Bagratid Armenia during the reign of Ashot III, between 952 and 977, and grew into a thriving economic and cultural center. Although the city lay along no earlier major trade route, its size, power, and wealth made it an important trading hub.
Wealthier Byzantine men hunted deer and wild boar with dogs and hawks, and sometimes trapped, netted, or lured birds with lime. Larger game animals counted as an expensive and rare source of meat.

Rye, millet, oats, and vetch were grown mainly as animal fodder in the Byzantine world rather than for human eating. Millet could still be boiled into a porridge called trachanas, made from this humble grain.

art.text: Construction of Zvartnots Cathedral began in 643 under the guidance of Catholicos Nerses III the Builder. The cathedral was noted for a circular exterior structure unique in medieval Armenian architecture, with interior piers upholding a multifloor structure crowned by a dome.

The Cathedral of Mren was built between 631 and 639 by David Saharuni, an Armenian ally of Byzantine Emperor Heraclius, to celebrate Heraclius's entry into Jerusalem in 628. It is the largest surviving domed basilica from seventh century Armenian architecture, and its frescoes depict the return of the True Cross to Jerusalem.

The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Aghtamar Island was built between 915 and 921 by the architect-monk Manuel for King Gagik I Artsruni of Vaspurakan. Made of pink volcanic tuff, its interior measures 14.80 by 11.5 meters, with the dome reaching 20.40 meters above ground.
art.source_title: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar

art.text: Churches built during the Bagratuni era expanded on seventh century designs, often rising steeper in elevation and introducing donor portraits carved in the round. Builders incorporated ideas from Byzantine and Islamic architecture, using stone construction with vaulted ceilings that supported spherical domes.

Zvartnots was dedicated to St. Gregory and built on the spot where King Trdat III and Gregory the Illuminator were said to have once met. When Nerses III left for Tayk between 653 and 659, construction of the cathedral continued under Anastas Akoratsi.

Mren's frescoes are a rare example of Byzantine art showing Emperor Heraclius dismounted from his horse and wearing plain clothing, referencing the legend that the True Cross grew too heavy until he removed his crown and royal robes. Inscriptions in the cathedral also named Bishop Theophilus and Prince Nerses Kamsarakan.

During Byzantine iconoclasm, from 730 to 843, the vast majority of icons were destroyed. So little remains that any discovery sheds new light. Most surviving works are in Italy or at Saint Catherine's Monastery in Egypt.

Zvartnots Cathedral stood for 320 years before collapsing in the tenth century, although it was engineered to last 1,000 years, a projected date for the second coming of Christ. Historians still debate how it fell, mostly arguing for an earthquake or for attacks arising from repeated Arab raids. Excavations have uncovered traces of large fires at the site, perhaps from an earlier attempt to destroy the church.

Following the decline of Byzantine power in the region, the Cathedral of Mren came under Muslim control for two centuries. It was reconsecrated once Christian rule returned to the area in the 10th to 11th century.

The exterior walls of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross are covered with an extensive array of bas-relief carvings, mostly of biblical scenes such as Eden, the serpent, and Adam and Eve. Some scholars say the friezes parallel Umayyad art, with a turbaned prince, Arab styles of dress and wine imagery, alongside Sassanian royal imagery such as griffins. After World War I the church was left largely ignored and exposed to extensive vandalism, and comparisons with pre-1914 photographs show damage to the relief carvings.
art.source_title: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar

art.text: The Persian geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih, who died in 911, wrote about instruments in the 9th century. He described the Byzantine lyra as a bowed instrument equivalent to the Arab rabab. He also listed other typical Byzantine instruments, including the urghun (organ) and the salandj (probably a bagpipe).

war.text: In 622, shocked by the loss of provinces such as Egypt and by Khosrow's refusal to make peace, Emperor Heraclius took direct command of the Byzantine army. He abandoned defence and began an offensive strategy against Persia.

Heraclius and the Byzantines eventually won their war with Persia, though the peace that followed proved illusory. His years of offensives, together with the failure to take Constantinople, brought down Khosrow II in 628. His son Kavad II took the throne and surrendered within a month, ordering his forces out of all Byzantine territory, including Anatolia.
Heraclius led his men into Cappadocia in 622 and defeated a Persian army under Shahrbaraz. The victory forced the Persians out of Anatolia and was described as much needed after a run of failures.

Heraclius's first offensive was cut short when the Pannonian Avars threatened Byzantine holdings in Thrace, and he spent two years dealing with them. Returning in 624, he attacked through Armenia into the Persian heartland on the Persian Plateau. He kept up the offensive for four years.

In 626, Constantinople was attacked by the Pannonian Avars together with Persian forces. Heraclius still did not return to defend it and kept up his offensives in the Persian heartland. The failure to take the city helped bring about the fall of Khosrow II.

Michael deposed Leo, but soon faced a revolt by a fellow military commander, Thomas the Slav, who claimed the throne. The resulting civil war dragged on until 824 and included a siege of Constantinople. It ended when Thomas was defeated and killed.

literature.text: The Turkish epic tradition properly begins with the Book of Dede Korkut. It is written in a language recognizably similar to modern Turkish, and it developed from the oral traditions of the Oghuz Turks.

Turkish folk literature stretches in a more or less unbroken line from about the 10th or 11th century CE to today. Because of this, it is best understood through three basic genres: epic, folk poetry and folklore.

The Turkish people first became Muslim sometime around the 9th or 10th century CE. From then on, Islam had an enormous influence on their society and literature, especially the mystically oriented Sufi and Shi'a varieties.

Greek was the main language both spoken and written in Anatolia until the end of the Byzantine era. That long Greek influence traced back to Greek city-states along the coasts, and it outlasted Roman rule.

science.text: Anania Shirakatsi, a 7th-century Armenian polymath, wrote works on mathematics, astronomy, geography and chronology and is considered the father of the exact and natural sciences in Armenia. He was the first Armenian mathematician, astronomer and cosmographer.

In mathematics, Anania Shirakatsi created the earliest known table of results for the four basic operations. He also compiled the earliest known collection of recreational math puzzles and the first book of math problems written in Armenian.

Anania Shirakatsi wrote the Ashkharhatsuyts, the first known geographic work in classical Armenian. It described Greater Armenia, Persia and the wider Caucasus, including Georgia and Caucasian Albania, in detail before the Arab invasions.
Anania Shirakatsi devised a system of mathematical notation based on the Armenian alphabet. He remained the only writer known to have ever used this notation system.

Anania studied for eight years under Tychicus, a scholar in Trebizond, in the 620s or 630s. Tychicus had served in the Byzantine army in Armenia, where he was wounded by the Persians and retired from the military. He then studied in Alexandria, Rome and Constantinople before returning to his native Trebizond and founding a school around 615 CE.

Many of Anania Shirakatsi's works were compiled into the K'nnikon, completed around 666 CE, which became the standard science textbook in medieval Armenia. Scholar Valentina Calzolari later described it as a monumental encyclopedic work.
About 40 works have been attributed to Anania Shirakatsi, though only around half of them survive today. They cover mathematics, astronomy, cosmology, geography, chronology and meteorology.

In Tychicus's library at Trebizond, Anania Shirakatsi found sacred and secular Greek texts on science, medicine, chronology and history, which he called everything, exoteric and esoteric. Anania considered Tychicus predestined by God to introduce science into Armenia.

The Ashkharhatsuyts is believed to have been written between 610 and 636 CE and survives in both long and short versions. Its description of Europe, North Africa and Asia draws on the now-lost geography of Pappus of Alexandria.

A separate work by Anania Shirakatsi, The Itinerary, described six routes from Dvin, Armenia's capital, to major settlements, giving distances in miles. These miles referred to the Arabic mile of 1,917.6 metres, and the work may originally have been part of the Ashkharhatsuyts.

politics.text: After the Muslim invasion of Syria and Egypt in 634 to 645, during the reign of Heraclius, Anatolia became vital to the Byzantine Empire. For the next two hundred and fifty years the region suffered constant raids by Arab Muslim forces, who came mainly from the cities of Antioch, Tarsus and Aleppo near the Anatolian borders.

In 622, after shocking losses of Roman provinces such as Egypt and Khosrow's refusal of peace, Heraclius took direct control of the Byzantine army. He led his men to Cappadocia and defeated a Persian army under Shahrbaraz, driving it out of Anatolia.

The Eastern Roman Empire reached its greatest extent in the 6th century under the emperor Justinian. Its survival for further centuries, even after it shrank, owed much to new military tactics and strategy, alliances, mercenary forces and reforms in governance.

From 526 to 532, the Sasanian Empire fought a war with the Byzantine Empire. It ended with the Treaty of Eternal Peace, under which the Sasanians kept Iberia, the Byzantines received Lazica and Persarmenia, and the Byzantines paid 11,000 pounds of gold a year in tribute.

Ani became the kingdom's capital during the reign of Ashot III, from 952 to 977, and grew into a thriving economic and cultural center. Situated on a major trade intersection between the Byzantines, Arabs and other merchants, the city had already earned renown for its legendary '40 gates and 1,001 churches' through its growth over the 9th century.

Heraclius's first offensive was interrupted by an attack from the Pannonian Avars, who threatened the empire's holding in Thrace. He spent the next two years dealing with that problem, then returned in 624 to renew his campaign against the Persians.

In 624 Heraclius attacked through Armenia into the Sassanid heartland on the Persian Plateau. He kept up the offensive for four years, and did not even return when Constantinople was attacked by the Pannonian Avars and Persian forces in 626.

Heraclius's offensives, the failure to conquer Constantinople and suspected intrigues against Shahrbaraz brought about the fall of Khosrow II. His son Kavad II was elevated in 628 and, within a month, surrendered to the Byzantines.
The Mihranid dynasty (630-705) came to rule Caucasian Albania in the early 7th century, with Partav as its centre. Varaz Grigor (628-642) took the title Prince of Albania.

politics.text: Kavad II ordered his forces to withdraw from all Byzantine territory, including Anatolia. Heraclius had defeated Persia and safeguarded Anatolia, but the source calls the peace illusory.

philosophy.text: Anania Shirakatsi was a 7th-century Armenian polymath and natural philosopher, one of the few secular scholars in medieval Armenia. He was educated by Tychicus in Trebizond and became part of the Armenian Hellenizing School, later called the father of the exact and natural sciences in Armenia.

Paulicianism was a Christian sect that originated in Armenia in the 7th century, traditionally founded by an Armenian named Constantine from a Syrian community near Samosata. It flourished between 650 and 872 along the Byzantine Empire's frontier with the Arab Caliphate in Armenia and Eastern Anatolia, despite intermittent persecutions and deportations by the imperial authorities. About twenty-seven years after founding his first congregation, Constantine was arrested, tried for heresy and stoned to death; his successor Simeon, who had been the court official who carried out the order, was burned to death in 690, the punishment pronounced upon the Manichaeans.

Maximus the Confessor was a Christian monk, theologian and Neoplatonic scholar who was persecuted for his views on Christ's human and divine will. After his second trial for heresy in 662 he was tortured: his tongue was cut out so he could no longer speak his rebellion, and his right hand was cut off so he could no longer write letters. He was exiled to the fortress of Schemarum, perhaps Muris-Tsikhe near Tsageri in present-day Georgia, and died soon after, on 13 August 662.

Gregory of Narek was an Armenian mystical poet, monk and theologian stationed at Narekavank on the southern shores of Lake Van, celebrated as the most beloved figure of Armenian religious tradition. He is best known for his Book of Lamentations, a mystical work still used as a confessional prayer book in Armenian households.

The term iconoclasm originates from the Byzantine Iconoclasm, the struggle between proponents and opponents of religious icons in the Byzantine Empire, from 726 to 842 AD. Those who supported destroying icons were called iconoclasts, while those who venerated them were known as iconodules.

The Tondrakians were an anti-feudal Christian sect founded by Smbat Zarehavantsi, centered on the district of Tondrak north of Lake Van, and flourished from the early 9th to the 11th century. They supported peasants' property rights and equality between men and women, and resembled the Paulician movement. Armenian feudal lords and clergy joined Arab emirs and Byzantines in persecuting them, most were deported to Thrace after defeats by Byzantium, and by the middle of the 11th century the Byzantine governor Gregory Magistros eliminated all remnants of the sect. Their critic Gregory of Narek also accused them of being sexually promiscuous.

The Council of Manzikert met in 726, convoked by the Armenian catholicos John of Odzun and attended by many Armenian bishops and six bishops of the Syriac church sent by Patriarch Athanasius III. Its canons anathematized the Aphthartodocetists, who believed Jesus' body was incorruptible, and some of the more heretical followers of Severus of Antioch. The council formally withdrew the Armenian church from communion with the Greek Orthodox church and affirmed Christ as a single hypostasis and single nature, holding that while his human body was capable of pain and suffering, "of his divine nature he was above suffering". After the council, Armenian Chalcedonism was suppressed.

In 843, Empress Theodora, as regent to her son Michael III, instituted a major persecution of the Paulicians throughout Asia Minor, in which 100,000 adherents in Byzantine Armenia alone were said to have lost their lives or property. In response, many Paulicians under their leader Karbeas fled across the border to Armenia under Arab control, where under the protection of Umar al-Aqta they built the fortress cities of Amara and Tephrike and set up an independent state. After prolonged warfare, with Karbeas's successor Chrysocheres devastating many cities and killed in battle in 872 or 878, the Byzantines destroyed the state of Tephrike in the 870s, and the survivors were largely displaced.

Before taking monastic vows, Maximus the Confessor served as a civil servant and aide to the Byzantine Emperor Heraclius, having studied the Platonic dialogues, the works of Aristotle, and later Neoplatonic commentators such as Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus and Proclus. He later gave up his position in politics to enter monastic life.

culture.text: Arab attacks reduced the territory Justinian had once held, and the Byzantine Empire lost much of its diversity in languages and religious views. Yet border regions such as Cappadocia saw an influx of Armenians, Jacobite Syrians and Georgians. Byzantine emperors invited them there as settlers.

Most of the old Anatolian languages were gradually replaced by Koine Greek. The poorly attested Isaurian language may have survived in the Taurus highlands into the sixth century AD. If so, it was possibly the last survivor of the Anatolian branch of Indo-European.

Turkic peoples began moving toward the land of modern Turkey during the main Turkic migration, which ran between the 6th and 11th centuries. It was part of a wider movement across Central Asia and into Europe and the Middle East. The Seljuks, who later conquered Byzantine Anatolia, arrived mainly in the eleventh century.

Noel Lenski argued that people of the Isaurian highlands kept speaking a branch of Luwian until at least the end of the sixth century. He cited a passage in the Life of Symeon Stylites that describes local people as speaking their "own dialect". If he is right, Isaurian outlasted every other known Anatolian language.

The case for a late Isaurian language is uncertain. There is no continuous Isaurian corpus, and an Isaurian regional identity in late antiquity does not prove the language was still spoken. Survival to around AD 600 is a scholarly possibility, not a securely established date, and survival far into the seventh century is not directly shown.
